title: The three kinds of gift
hookLine: the Gita sorts gifts into three kinds, and only one needs no thank-you
carry: the sattvic gift expects nothing back

cards: A twenty-dollar bill can be three completely different gifts. Handed over with a little speech about how generous this is. Pushed across the table with a sigh, because saying no would be awkward.
Or slipped to the right person, at the right moment, with no one keeping score. In chapter seventeen of the Gita, Arjuna asks about people who worship with faith but outside the scriptures' rules.
Krishna answers by sorting faith, food, sacrifice and discipline by the three gunas, the qualities that run through everything, and giving gets three verses. Same bill, three gifts.

teach.b: The gunas are sattva, clarity and balance; rajas, restless drive; and tamas, heaviness and dullness. Here are the three gifts, in paraphrase.

teach.h: SATTVIC: RIGHT, NO RETURN, RIGHT TIME, RIGHT PERSON.
teach.b: The sattvic gift is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can do nothing in return, at the right place and time, to a fitting person.

teach.h: RAJASIC: TO GET BACK, OR GRUDGING.
teach.b: The rajasic gift is given to get something back, or with an eye to some reward, or grudgingly.
The tamasic gift is given at the wrong place and time, to the wrong person, without respect, with contempt. Look at what the first gift asks for. Not size; the verse doesn't mention an amount at all.
Four things: the right reason, which is that it's right; no return; the right timing; and the right person. That last part keeps it from being careless. Giving well takes attention.
Who actually needs this? Is now the moment, or would next month be better for them? The second gift isn't evil.
It's just tangled up with getting, and the Gita puts giving with reluctance in it, which is honest about how giving can feel. The third comes with contempt, so whatever it helps with, it also wounds.

This is the measure many Hindus hold their own giving to, at a festival, a temple, a family occasion: not how much, but whether anything is expected back. Before you give, the Gita would have you ask four questions.
Why am I giving? What am I expecting back? When is the right time?
To whom? Dana, the gift, is part of Hindu practice.
Chapter seventeen asks that it be done with clear eyes.

how: Dana, giving, is part of Hindu practice at festivals, temple visits and family occasions, and some Hindus point to the Gita's description of the sattvic gift, given without expecting return, when they talk about how to give.

o: a gift made loudly so others see your generosity
a gift given because it's right, expecting nothing back
a fixed sum every household must pay the temple

p: given because it's right, nothing back
given to get back, or grudgingly
given with contempt, at the wrong time

s: the Gita says the best gift is the largest one
the verse on the sattvic gift never mentions an amount.
in chapter seventeen, giving grudgingly counts as rajasic
the rajasic gift is given to get something back, or reluctantly.
the sattvic gift goes to someone who can do nothing in return
that's one of its marks, with the right place, time and person.

games.q: you want to give, and you want it to count as the Gita's sattvic gift. what matters most?
o: that it's large enough to be noticed.
that it's given because it's right, expecting nothing, to the right person at the right time.
that the person knows exactly who gave it.
games.why: Gita 17.20 names no amount. It asks for the right reason, no return, the right place and time, and a fitting person.

practice: Bring to mind one gift you've given recently, money, time, a favor, a meal, and hold it up to the four questions gently, without scoring yourself: why, what back, when, to whom.

Then picture one gift you might give in the coming weeks, ask the same four questions, and see if any answer shifts. If you pray, you can offer that future gift to the one you pray to before it's given.

wordCard.voice: Dana. The gift, given because it's right, with nothing expected back, at the right time, to the right person.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dana, the gift or giving. Gita 17.20–22 sorts it by the three gunas.

carryVoice: Your line: the sattvic gift expects nothing back. Not one of its marks is how much. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 17.20–17.22 (the sattvic, rajasic and tamasic gift)
Bhagavad Gita 17.2–17.10 (the three gunas applied to faith and food, as context for the chapter)
Bhagavad Gita 17.1 (Arjuna's question about those who worship with faith but set aside the scriptures' rules)
